analysis.one_liner: Extends health programs, forces drug-rebate and fee transparency, and expands recycling and fuel choices.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2025 and sent to five House committees, the bill has no cosponsors and no committee has taken any action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill bundles together many separate ideas. On health, it keeps funding and rules going for community health centers, rural hospital and doctor payments, Medicare telehealth, substance-use-disorder treatment, and pandemic preparedness, lets more seniors with disabilities qualify for Medicaid, and requires pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen between drugmakers and insurers — to pass every dollar of rebates back to health plans. On consumer matters, it requires hotels and ticket sellers to show the full price up front, criminalizes sharing intimate images without consent, requires disclosure of cameras and microphones in smart devices, and bans retail products with high concentrations of sodium nitrite. On the environment and energy, it funds recycling and drinking-water projects, renews diesel-emissions grants, and lets gasoline blended with 10-15% ethanol be sold year-round.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passes, the main winners are ordinary people: seniors whose Medicare telehealth coverage and home-hospital care would continue, people with disabilities seeking Medicaid, community health centers and their patients, people in treatment for substance use disorders, and rural residents whose hospitals and pharmacies keep higher payments. Consumers also gain from all-in pricing on tickets and hotel rooms, and from the ban on spreading nonconsensual intimate images. Fuel retailers and drivers who want ethanol-blended gasoline get year-round access.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would allow people 65 and over with a medically improved disability to qualify for Medicaid, and it extends higher Medicare payments for rural and low-volume hospitals and doctors so more keep operating in underserved areas.

It reauthorizes community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, and a wide range of substance-use-disorder and mental health programs, which fund care for people who otherwise often go without it.

It would require pharmacy benefit managers to remit 100% of prescription drug rebates to the health plans they serve, and it bans the abusive 'spread pricing' practice in Medicaid in which the middleman pockets the difference.

It requires all-inclusive ticket price disclosure for concerts, bans advertising hotel rooms without the full price, and makes it a federal crime to publish intimate images of someone without consent.
It creates grant programs for recycling access in underserved communities and drinking-water infrastructure, and reauthorizes diesel-emissions-reduction grants.

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies, which would lose their rebate share and Medicaid spread-pricing margins; on hotels and ticketing platforms, which must show full prices; on sellers of e-bike and mobility batteries, which must meet federal safety standards; and on federal taxpayers, who fund the extended Medicare payments and reauthorized grant programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy middlemen, hotels, ticket sellers, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Much of the bill is not new help but a renewal of health programs and provider payment increases that were already set to expire, adding federal Medicare and Medicaid spending without restructuring how the money is spent.

The ethanol provision permanently removes seasonal limits on selling gasoline blended with 10-15% ethanol, which mainly benefits the ethanol and corn industries and the fuel retailers that sell their product, alongside modest consumer fuel choice.

The sodium nitrite ban applies only to retail consumer products and expressly exempts food, meat, poultry, and eggs, so it addresses a narrow poisoning risk rather than the chemical in processed food.

Requiring pharmacy benefit managers to turn over 100% of rebates to plans would cut a major revenue stream; industry and some economists argue the money could resurface as higher plan premiums if not paired with cost rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer and patient provisions are real and mostly popular: keeping telehealth and rural-hospital payments alive, exposing junk fees, cracking down on image abuse. The main honest caveat is that this is largely a renewal bill — it extends existing spending rather than delivering new savings, and the eye-catching cost-lowering provisions (rebate pass-through, spread-pricing ban) are aimed at one slice of the drug-pricing problem rather than drug list prices themselves. The ethanol rider is the clearest provision serving an industry rather than consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2025 and split among five House committees, and none of them has scheduled a hearing or a vote; with no cosponsors, it has not moved since.

narrative.text: Representative Frank Pallone of New Jersey introduced the bill on March 3, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to five House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Budget, Judiciary, and Education and Workforce — with no schedule set for consideration.
No members of either party have signed on as cosponsors.
The congressional record shows no further action: no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion activity in the provided record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody has moved: the current payment rules, rebate arrangements, and fee practices continue unchanged. The industries the bill would restrict — pharmacy benefit managers, hotels, ticket resellers — keep the status quo, while the programs waiting for renewal keep running on temporary extensions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; affected industries keep the status quo

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: U.S. Representative, NJ-06 (sponsor; senior Democrat on Energy and Commerce)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to five committees; no cosponsors have joined.

sides.party_line_note: Only the Democratic sponsor has acted so far; no cosponsors from either party and no committee action, so the partisan shape of the fight has not yet formed.

industries.note: The bill forces PBMs to hand 100% of drug rebates to health plans and bans Medicaid spread pricing, where the middleman profits on the gap between what it pays pharmacies and what it bills the state. Those are the core of the PBM business model's margin on prescription drugs.

industries.industry: Hospitals and physicians (especially rural and low-volume)
industries.note: The bill extends higher Medicare payments for rural and low-volume hospitals, the Medicare-dependent hospital program, and ambulance add-ons, which keeps facilities open in areas that would otherwise lose care — but it does so by continuing federal spending rather than reforming payment.

industries.industry: Community health centers and safety-net providers
industries.note: Reauthorization of community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, teaching health centers, and substance-use-disorder treatment programs renews funding for care to uninsured and underserved patients.

industries.industry: Ethanol producers, corn growers, and fuel retailers
industries.note: The Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act provision lets E10-E15 gasoline blends be sold year-round nationwide, expanding the market for ethanol-blended fuel. Drivers get fuel choice, but the main beneficiary is the biofuel supply chain.
The Hotel Fees Transparency Act prohibits advertising a room price that omits mandatory fees, ending the practice of quoting a low rate and adding resort fees at checkout.

The bill requires all-inclusive ticket price display, bans speculative ticketing, and mandates refunds, hitting secondary market practices that currently let buyers discover hidden charges late in checkout.

Mandatory adoption of existing UL safety standards for light electric vehicle batteries raises compliance costs but targets lithium-ion battery fires in e-bikes and scooters that have injured riders and damaged apartment buildings.

analysis.trajectory: A five-committee referral with no cosponsors makes standalone action very unlikely. However, most of its provisions are versions of health 'extender' and consumer bills that have moved with bipartisan support in past Congresses, so individual pieces — Medicare telehealth, hospital payment extenders, PBM rebate reform, ticket-fee disclosure — are more likely to advance folded into a larger health or appropriations package than as this bill itself.
